title: JWT Authentication Deep Dive
content:
JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are a compact, URL-safe way to represent claims between two parties. A JWT consists of three parts: header, payload, and signature, separated by dots.

The header specifies the signing algorithm (for example HS256 or RS256). The payload contains claims such as sub, exp, iat, and custom application data. The signature is created by signing the base64-encoded header and payload using a secret (HMAC) or a private key (RSA/ECDSA).

JWTs are often used in stateless authentication systems where the server does not store session state. Instead, the token carries identity and authorization claims.

Security considerations:
- Always validate the signature, algorithm, issuer/audience (if used), and expiration (exp).
- Avoid storing sensitive data in the payload because it is only encoded, not encrypted.
- Use short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens for longer sessions.
- Prefer RS256 (asymmetric) in distributed systems to avoid sharing a single secret across services.

A common mistake is storing access tokens in localStorage, which increases the impact of XSS. A safer option is HttpOnly cookies with CSRF defenses (SameSite, CSRF token, and careful CORS settings).

Revocation is another common pitfall. With stateless JWTs, immediate revocation is hard. Typical mitigations are short expirations, server-side refresh token revocation lists, and rotating refresh tokens.

Finally, be careful with clock skew and token validation. Some systems apply a small leeway window to avoid rejecting tokens due to time drift, but do not make the leeway too large

title: REST vs GraphQL APIs
content:
REST APIs are resource-based and usually expose multiple endpoints like /users, /orders, or /products. Each endpoint typically returns a fixed response structure.

GraphQL exposes a single endpoint and lets clients request exactly the fields they need. This can reduce over-fetching and under-fetching, especially in frontend-heavy applications.

Key differences:
- REST: multiple endpoints, fixed shapes, relies on HTTP semantics (status codes, caching headers).
- GraphQL: single endpoint, flexible shapes, errors often returned in a standard errors array, and HTTP status is frequently 200 even when query-level errors exist.

Caching:
REST is easier to cache with standard HTTP caches (ETag, Cache-Control). GraphQL is harder to cache at the transport layer because many queries go to the same endpoint. GraphQL caching often moves to the client (normalized caches) or requires persisted queries.

Operational complexity:
GraphQL introduces schema design, resolvers, and query complexity management. Without limits, nested queries can become expensive. Mitigations include depth limits, complexity scoring, query whitelisting (persisted queries), and rate limiting.

When REST is better:
- Simple CRUD services
- Strong reliance on HTTP caching
- Teams preferring simpler operational tooling

When GraphQL is better:
- Multiple clients with different data needs
- Rapid iteration on frontend requirements
- Complex data graphs where composing multiple REST calls becomes painful

title: React Rendering and Performance Optimization
content:
React re-renders a component when its state changes, when its props change, or when its parent re-renders and passes new references. React uses a virtual DOM diff to compute minimal DOM updates.

Common performance problems come from unnecessary re-renders:
- Inline object and function props cause new references each render.
- Large lists re-render on every keystroke.
- State stored too high in the tree causes many descendants to update.

Optimizations:
- React.memo: memoize pure components so they only re-render when props change.
- useMemo: memoize expensive computations, derived lists, and filtered results.
- useCallback: memoize functions passed down to children, preventing prop reference changes.

List keys:
Stable keys are essential. Using array indexes as keys can cause incorrect UI behavior during insertions/reordering, and can break component state.

State placement:
Store state as close as possible to where it is used. For shared state, consider context, but be careful: context updates re-render all consumers. For large apps, selective state management patterns or splitting contexts helps.

Profiling:
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify slow commits and components that re-render too often. In many cases, the best optimization is simplifying data flow and reducing rendering work rather than premature memoization.

Practical tip:
Optimize only after measuring. Memoization adds complexity and can be counterproductive if dependencies change frequently.

title: Docker Containers Explained
content:
Docker runs applications in isolated environments called containers. A container packages the application with its dependencies and runtime configuration.

Containers vs virtual machines:
- Virtual machines include a full guest OS per VM.
- Containers share the host OS kernel, making them smaller and faster to start.

Core concepts:
- Image: an immutable template built from layers (often from a Dockerfile).
- Container: a running instance of an image.
- Volume: persistent storage that lives outside the container lifecycle.
- Network: allows containers to communicate, with DNS-based discovery in many setups.

Dockerfile basics:
A Dockerfile describes how to build an image: base image, copying app files, installing dependencies, and defining the startup command.

Why teams use Docker:
- Consistent environments across dev/staging/prod
- Easier onboarding and reproducible builds
- Works well with CI pipelines

Gotchas:
- Containers still require security updates and monitoring.
- Do not bake secrets into images.
- Be mindful of file permissions, volume mounts, and host networking.

For local development, Docker Compose is often used to run multi-service setups (API, database, cache) with a single command.

title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Flows
content:
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows an application to access resources on behalf of a user without sharing the user's password. OAuth defines roles like Resource Owner, Client, Authorization Server, and Resource Server.

Common flows:
- Authorization Code Flow: recommended for server-rendered web apps.
- Authorization Code with PKCE: recommended for SPAs and mobile apps. PKCE mitigates authorization code interception.
- Client Credentials Flow: service-to-service calls where no user is involved.

Implicit Flow is deprecated for modern SPAs due to security concerns.

Important details:
- Redirect URIs must be strict and validated.
- Scopes should be minimal (least privilege).
- Access tokens should be short-lived; refresh tokens require careful storage and rotation.

OAuth vs Authentication:
OAuth itself is not authentication. For authentication, OpenID Connect (OIDC) extends OAuth with an ID token and standard identity claims.

Common misconfigurations:
- Overly broad scopes
- Insecure redirect URI patterns
- Weak token storage choices in the browser

For SPAs:
Use PKCE + Authorization Code flow, store tokens carefully, and ensure CORS and cookie settings are correct if using HttpOnly cookies.

title: Linux Process Management Basics
content:
In Linux, a running program is a process identified by a PID (process ID). You can inspect processes using ps, top, or htop. Each process has a state (running, sleeping, stopped, zombie) and resource usage.

Signals are a primary mechanism to control processes:
- SIGTERM: request graceful shutdown (default for kill).
- SIGKILL: immediate termination (cannot be caught).
- SIGINT: interrupt (Ctrl+C) for foreground processes.

Job control:
- Run a command in the background by appending &: for example, "myapp &".
- Suspend a foreground process with Ctrl+Z.
- Resume with fg (foreground) or bg (background).

Practical tips:
- Prefer SIGTERM before SIGKILL to allow cleanup.
- Use pgrep to find PIDs by name.
- Use systemd service files for long-running daemons in production environments.

Understanding processes and signals helps debug runaway CPU usage, memory leaks, and stuck programs, and is a core skill for troubleshooting servers.

title: Organizational Information Security Policy
content:
Information security is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and data from digital attacks, unauthorized access, and damage. Every employee in a technology company plays a direct role in keeping organizational assets safe.

Core Concepts
The three pillars of information security are known as the CIA Triad:
- Confidentiality: ensuring information is accessible only to authorized individuals.
- Integrity: ensuring data is accurate and has not been tampered with.
- Availability: ensuring systems and data are accessible when needed.

Your Responsibilities as an Employee
Security is everyone's job. Your key obligations include: locking your workstation when stepping away, never sharing login credentials, reporting suspicious emails or activity to the security team, and following the clean desk policy for sensitive documents.

Information Classification Levels
The organization classifies all data into four levels — Public, Internal, Confidential, and Top Secret. Each level determines who can access the data, how it must be stored, and whether it can leave the organization. When in doubt about a document's classification, treat it as Confidential until confirmed otherwise.

Acceptable Use
Company devices and networks are for business use. Limited personal use is tolerated but must not involve installing unauthorized software, accessing inappropriate content, or connecting to unsecured public Wi-Fi without VPN.

Violations and Enforcement
Violations of this policy range from minor (handled via coaching) to severe (immediate termination). Examples of severe violations include intentionally sharing confidential data externally, disabling security controls, or failing to report a known incident.

title: Phishing and Social Engineering Defense
content:
Phishing is the most common entry point for cyberattacks. It works by tricking people — not by breaking technical defenses. Understanding how these attacks look and feel is your best protection.

What Attackers Want
Attackers use phishing to steal credentials, install malware, transfer money fraudulently, or gain a foothold inside your organization's systems. The goal is always access — to your account, your data, or your network.

The Anatomy of a Phishing Email
A typical phishing email has: a sender address that looks almost right but isn't, a subject line designed to create urgency or fear, a call to action (click a link, open an attachment, reply with information), and branding that mimics a trusted company or colleague.

Spear Phishing — Targeted Attacks
Spear phishing is a personalized version of phishing. Attackers research their target on LinkedIn, company websites, and social media before crafting a message that references real names, projects, or internal terminology. These attacks are harder to detect and more likely to succeed.

Vishing — Phone-Based Attacks
Vishing (voice phishing) involves a caller impersonating IT support, a bank, a vendor, or even a senior executive. They create urgency ("your account is being attacked right now") and ask you to reveal a password, approve an MFA request, or install remote access software.

The Golden Rule
When in doubt, do not act. Pause, verify through a separate channel, and contact the security team. A legitimate sender will never mind you taking time to confirm their identity.

title: Password Management and Multi-Factor Authentication
content:
Passwords and multi-factor authentication (MFA) are the first line of defense for every account in the organization. Most account takeovers start with a weak, reused, or stolen password, and most of them are stopped by MFA.

Password Requirements
Every account must use a unique password of at least 14 characters. Length matters more than complexity: a long passphrase made of several unrelated words is stronger and easier to remember than a short password full of symbols. Never reuse a work password on any other site, and never share it with anyone, including IT support or a manager.

Use the Company Password Manager
The approved password manager generates, stores, and fills strong passwords for you. Store every work credential there, never in browser notes, spreadsheets, or sticky notes. Shared team credentials, such as a vendor portal login, belong in a shared vault with named access, not in chat messages or email.

Multi-Factor Authentication
MFA requires a second proof of identity in addition to the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough to log in. MFA is mandatory for email, VPN, cloud consoles, source control, and every SaaS tool that supports it.

Choosing an MFA Method
From strongest to weakest: hardware security keys (FIDO2, such as YubiKey), authenticator apps with number matching, and SMS codes. Hardware keys cannot be phished and are required for all administrator accounts. SMS is allowed only as a temporary fallback, because phone numbers can be hijacked through SIM swapping.

MFA Fatigue Attacks
Attackers who already have a password may send repeated push requests, hoping the user approves one to make them stop. Never approve an MFA request you did not start. If you receive unexpected requests, deny them, change your password, and report it to the security team immediately.

If Your Password Is Exposed
Change the password right away, sign out of all active sessions, check the account for unfamiliar activity, and open a high priority ticket. Reporting quickly is always better than hoping nothing happened.

title: Cloud Security and SaaS Protection
content:
Cloud computing allows organizations to run infrastructure, store data, and deliver services without owning physical hardware. With that flexibility comes a new security model — one where your team is responsible for securing what you build and configure on top of the cloud provider's platform.

The Shared Responsibility Model.
The cloud provider secures the underlying infrastructure — the physical data centers, networking hardware, and virtualization layer. Your organization secures everything built on top: your data, your applications, your access controls, and your configurations. Most cloud breaches happen not because the provider was hacked, but because a customer misconfigured a resource.

Identity Is the New Perimeter.
In cloud environments there is no traditional network perimeter. Anyone with valid credentials can access resources from anywhere. This is why Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the single most important security control in the cloud. Every user, service, and application should have only the permissions it needs — nothing more.

Common Misconfigurations to Avoid.
The most common cloud security mistakes include: leaving S3 buckets or blob storage publicly accessible, allowing 0.0.0.0/0 inbound rules in security groups, storing secrets or API keys in source code or environment variables, and running databases without encryption or with public endpoints.

SaaS Application Risks.
Every SaaS tool your team connects to is a potential entry point. Key controls for SaaS: enable SSO and MFA, review connected OAuth apps regularly (revoke anything unused), ensure off boarding removes access to every service, and avoid connecting SaaS tools with overly broad permissions.

Monitoring and Alerting
Logging must be enabled on all cloud accounts. Route logs to a central SIEM. Configure alerts for high-risk events such as: new IAM user creation, changes to security groups or firewall rules, API calls from unusual geolocations, and deletion of critical resources.

title: Secure Code and Secure SDLC
content:
Security in software development is not a final step before release — it is a continuous practice woven through every stage of building software. Catching a vulnerability during design costs almost nothing. Catching it in production can cost millions.

Shift Left — Security from the Start
Shift Left means moving security activities earlier in the development lifecycle. Instead of security reviews happening only at the end, they happen at every stage: requirements, design, implementation, testing, and deployment. Every developer is responsible for the security of their own code.

The Most Common Vulnerabilities
The OWASP Top 10 defines the most critical web application risks. The most frequently exploited include: SQL and command injection (unsanitized user input executed as code), broken access control (users accessing resources they shouldn't), and security misconfiguration (default credentials, open ports, verbose error messages).

Secrets Must Never Live in Code
API keys, database passwords, tokens, and certificates must never appear in source code, committed config files, or log output. Use a dedicated Secrets Manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and inject secrets at runtime via environment variables in your CI/CD system. Add pre-commit hooks to detect and block accidental secret commits.

Automated Security in CI/CD
Every pull request should trigger: SAST (static code analysis for vulnerabilities), SCA (dependency scanning for known CVEs), and secrets detection. DAST should run on staging environments before every major release. These checks are non-blocking for warnings but blocking for critical findings.

Code Review with a Security Lens
When reviewing code, ask: Does this endpoint validate and sanitize all inputs? Does it enforce authorization on every request? Could an error message expose internal details? Are external dependencies up to date? Security-focused questions should be part of every PR review, not a separate process.

title: Security Incident Response
content:
An incident response plan defines how the organization detects, contains, investigates, and recovers from security incidents. Having a clear plan before an incident occurs dramatically reduces damage and recovery time.

What Counts as an Incident
A security incident is any confirmed or suspected event that threatens the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of organizational assets. This includes malware infection, unauthorized access, data leakage, ransomware, DDoS attacks, and insider threats. Even a failed attack attempt should be logged and reviewed.

Report First, Fix Later
The single most important rule: report the incident to the security team before attempting to fix it. Well-intentioned actions -deleting a suspicious file, rebooting a compromised machine, or wiping a drive - can destroy forensic evidence that is critical to understanding what happened. Report first, then act under guidance.

The PICERL Framework
Incident response follows six stages: Preparation (tools, training, and runbooks ready before anything happens), Identification (confirming an incident occurred and classifying it), Containment (stopping the spread without destroying evidence), Eradication (removing the threat from the environment), Recovery (restoring systems safely), and Lessons Learned (documenting what happened and improving).

Severity Levels
Incidents are classified P1 through P4. P1 (Critical) includes active breaches, ransomware, and customer data exposure — immediate escalation to CISO. P2 (High) covers suspected unauthorized access and critical vulnerabilities in production. P3 (Medium) handles contained malware and failed attacks. P4 (Low) covers unverified suspicions and minor policy violations.

Every employee is a potential first responder. If you notice something unusual — a slow machine, an unfamiliar process, a strange login alert — report it. Your early alert could be the difference between a contained incident and a full breach.

title: Data Privacy, GDPR and CCPA
content:
Data privacy laws give individuals control over their personal information and impose obligations on organizations that collect and process it. Understanding these laws is essential for every employee who handles customer, employee, or partner data.

Personal Data — What It Includes
Personal data is any information that can identify a living individual, directly or indirectly. This includes obvious data like names and email addresses, but also IP addresses, cookie identifiers, device IDs, location data, and any combination of attributes that together identify someone.

GDPR in Plain Language
The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) applies to any organization processing personal data of EU residents. Its core message: collect only what you need, be transparent about how you use it, keep it secure, and delete it when you no longer need it. Violations can result in fines of up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover — whichever is higher.

Lawful Basis — You Need a Reason to Collect Data
You cannot collect or use personal data just because it would be useful. You need a lawful basis: consent from the individual, a contract that requires it, a legal obligation, or a legitimate business interest that doesn't override individual rights. The basis must be documented before processing begins.

Data Subject Rights
Individuals have the right to access their data, correct inaccuracies, request deletion, restrict processing, receive their data in a portable format, and object to certain types of processing. Requests must be responded to within 30 days. The organization must have a clear process for handling these requests.

Privacy by Design
Privacy should be built into products from the beginning, not added as an afterthought. This means collecting minimal data, defaulting to the most private settings, giving users genuine control, and conducting Privacy Impact Assessments before launching any feature that processes personal data.

title: Northwind Employee Handbook
content:
Northwind Logistics Employee Handbook

This handbook is a test document written for evaluating the InsightDesk assistant. Northwind Logistics is a fictional company.

1. Welcome and Purpose

Welcome to Northwind Logistics. This handbook explains how we work, what we expect from each other, and where to find help. It is meant to be read once during your first week and used as a reference afterward. If something in this handbook is unclear, ask your direct manager or the people operations team. The handbook is reviewed once a year, and the latest version always replaces earlier ones.

2. Working Hours and Attendance

Standard working hours are 09:00 to 17:30, Sunday to Thursday, with a 45 minute unpaid lunch break. Teams may agree on flexible start times between 08:00 and 10:00 as long as the core hours of 10:00 to 16:00 are covered. Employees record their attendance in the time tracking tool at the start and end of each day. Missing entries must be corrected by the end of the following working day. Repeated unexplained absences are handled by the direct manager together with people operations.

3. IT Help Desk

The IT help desk is open Sunday to Thursday, from 08:00 to 18:00. Requests are submitted through the internal ticket portal, and each ticket receives an automatic confirmation number. Urgent issues that block your work should be marked as high priority. The help desk handles laptop problems, account access, software requests, and printer issues. It does not handle personal devices or home internet problems. Typical response time for normal tickets is one working day.

4. Accounts and Passwords

Every employee receives a personal company account. Accounts are protected by a password of at least 14 characters and by multi-factor authentication. Passwords must be changed every 120 days. Sharing passwords between colleagues is not allowed under any circumstances. If you suspect your account was used by someone else, change your password immediately and open a high priority ticket. Shared mailboxes use delegated access instead of shared passwords.

5. Equipment and Laptops

New employees receive a company laptop, a docking station, and a headset. Laptops use full disk encryption, and this setting must never be disabled. Equipment remains the property of the company and must be returned on the last working day. Lost or stolen equipment must be reported to the help desk within 24 hours. Employees are responsible for reasonable care of their equipment, including keeping it away from food and drinks.

6. Software Installation

Only software from the approved catalog may be installed on company laptops. If you need a tool that is not in the catalog, submit a software request with a short business reason. The security team reviews each request and usually answers within five working days. Browser extensions count as software and follow the same process. Pirated or cracked software is strictly forbidden and may lead to disciplinary action.

7. Email Etiquette

Use clear subject lines and keep messages short. Reply to internal emails within two working days, even if only to say that you need more time. Do not use reply all unless everyone on the thread needs your answer. Avoid sending large attachments, and share links to the document storage instead. Messages that contain customer data must be sent only to approved recipients.

8. Meetings

Meetings should have an agenda and a clear owner. Invitations are sent at least one day in advance, except for urgent matters. Meetings start and end on time, and notes with action items are shared within one working day. Recurring meetings are reviewed every quarter, and those that no longer provide value are cancelled. Camera use in video meetings is encouraged but not required.

9. Travel and Expenses

Business travel must be approved by the direct manager before booking. Flights and hotels are booked through the approved travel agency. Employees submit expense reports with receipts within 30 days of the expense. Meals are reimbursed up to a daily limit that is published on the finance page. Personal expenses, such as entertainment or minibar purchases, are not reimbursed. Questions about expenses go to the finance team.

10. Leave and Holidays

Full time employees receive 22 days of paid annual leave per year, in addition to public holidays. Leave requests are submitted in the people system and approved by the direct manager. Up to five unused days may be carried over to the next year. Leave of more than ten consecutive working days should be planned at least a month in advance. Teams are expected to arrange coverage before leaving.

11. Sick Leave

Employees who are unwell should notify their direct manager as early as possible on the first day of absence. A medical certificate is required for absences of more than two consecutive days. Sick leave is paid according to local law. Employees should not work while ill unless they choose to and feel able. Information about your health is confidential and is shared only with people operations when necessary.

12. Remote Work

Northwind supports remote work for roles where it is practical. Employees may work remotely up to two days per week. Requests for remote work days must be submitted at least five working days in advance and approved by the direct manager. Remote employees must be reachable during core hours and must work from a private location. Company laptops are the only devices allowed for work with customer data. Working from another country is not permitted without written approval from people operations.

13. Office Access and Badges

Each employee receives a personal access badge on the first day. Badges must be worn visibly inside the office and must never be lent to another person. A lost badge should be reported to the facilities desk right away so that it can be blocked. Replacement badges are issued within one working day. Access to the server room and the finance area is limited to named employees and reviewed every six months.

14. Visitors

All visitors must be registered at the reception desk before entering the office. Visitors receive a temporary badge and must be accompanied by their host at all times. Hosts are responsible for the behavior of their visitors. Visitors may use the guest network but never the internal network. Photography inside the office is not allowed without permission. Deliveries are accepted only at the reception desk.

15. Data Classification

Company information is divided into four levels: public, internal, confidential, and restricted. Public information may be shared freely. Internal information stays within the company. Confidential information, such as customer contracts, is shared only with those who need it for their work. Restricted information, such as employee salaries and security reports, requires explicit approval for every access. When in doubt, treat the information as one level higher than you think.

16. Customer Communication

Customers are our most important partners, and every message to them reflects on the company. Respond to customer requests within one working day. Be honest about delays and problems, and propose a next step. Do not promise delivery dates that you cannot confirm with the operations team. Complaints are logged in the customer system and followed up by the service manager. Never share information about one customer with another.

17. Procurement

Purchases above a defined amount require at least two price quotes and approval from the department head. Contracts with suppliers are reviewed by the legal team before signing. Employees may not sign contracts on behalf of the company unless they have written signing authority. Gifts from suppliers above a symbolic value must be declined or reported to the compliance officer. Supplier performance is reviewed once a year.

18. Training and Development

Each employee has an annual learning budget that can be used for courses, conferences, and books. Training requests are agreed with the direct manager. New employees complete mandatory courses on security awareness and workplace conduct during the first month. Employees who attend external training are encouraged to share what they learned with their team. Internal mentoring is available and can be requested through people operations.

19. Performance Reviews

Performance is discussed twice a year, in a mid year check in and a full annual review. Employees write a short self assessment before each review. Managers give specific examples of strengths and areas to improve. Goals for the next period are agreed together and written down. Pay changes and promotions are decided after the annual review cycle and are not discussed during the mid year check in.

20. Health and Safety

Everyone is responsible for a safe workplace. Report hazards such as wet floors, damaged cables, or blocked exits to the facilities desk. The office has first aid kits on every floor, and a list of trained first aiders is posted next to each kit. Workstations should be set up ergonomically, and the facilities team can adjust chairs and desks on request. Employees are encouraged to take short breaks from screens during the day.

21. Emergency Procedures

In case of a fire alarm, stop working, leave the building by the nearest exit, and do not use the elevators. Do not return to the building until the building warden says that it is safe. Floor wardens check their floors and report to the building warden. In case of a medical emergency, call the national emergency number first and then notify the facilities desk. Evacuation drills are held once a year, and participation is mandatory.

22. Facilities Maintenance

The facilities desk is open Sunday to Thursday, from 07:00 to 16:00, and handles heating, lighting, cleaning, and repairs. Office cleaning takes place every evening after working hours. Kitchen supplies are refilled twice a week. Maintenance requests are submitted through the same ticket portal as IT requests, using the facilities category. Planned maintenance that may affect work, such as water or power shutdowns, is announced at least three working days in advance.

The backup power generator is tested every second Tuesday of the month at 06:30, before the office opens. During the test the lights may flicker briefly, and no action is required from employees.

23. Closing

Thank you for reading this handbook. Our workplace works best when everyone takes responsibility, asks questions early, and helps colleagues. If you have suggestions for improving this handbook, send them to people operations. We wish you a successful and enjoyable time at Northwind Logistics.
